title: Chapter 81 — The Pequod Meets The Virgin
paragraphs: The fated day arrived, and we duly met the ship Jungfrau, captained by Derick De Deer, out of Bremen.
Once the greatest whaling people in the world, the Dutch and Germans are now among the least. But here and there, at very wide intervals across the Pacific, you still occasionally see their flag.

For some reason, the Jungfrau seemed quite eager to pay her respects. While still some distance from the Pequod, she rounded to and dropped a boat. Her captain stood impatiently in the bow instead of the stern, urging his men toward us.
"What has he got in his hand there?" cried Starbuck, pointing to something the German was waving. "Impossible! A lamp-feeder!"

"Not that," said Stubb. "No, no, it's a coffee-pot, Mr. Starbuck. He's coming over to make us our coffee, that German. Don't you see that big tin can beside him? That's his boiling water. Oh, he's all right, that German."
"Go on with you," cried Flask. "It's a lamp-feeder and an oil-can. He's out of oil and has come begging."

However curious it may seem for an oil-ship to be borrowing oil on the whaling-ground, and however much it may contradict the old proverb about carrying coals to Newcastle, sometimes such a thing really happens. And in the present case, Captain Derick De Deer was indeed carrying a lamp-feeder, just as Flask had said.

As he climbed onto the deck, Ahab abruptly confronted him, paying no attention to what he held. But in his broken English, the German quickly showed his complete ignorance of the White Whale. He immediately turned the conversation to his lamp-feeder and oil-can, remarking that he had to turn into his hammock at night in total darkness. His last drop of Bremen oil was gone, and not a single flying-fish had been captured to make up the difference. He finished by hinting that his ship was indeed what the Fishery technically calls a clean one — that is, an empty one — well deserving the name of Jungfrau, or the Virgin.

His needs supplied, Derick departed. But he had not yet reached his ship when whales were spotted almost simultaneously from the mastheads of both vessels. Derick was so eager for the chase that without pausing to put his oil-can and lamp-feeder aboard, he swung his boat around and went after the great lamp-feeders themselves.

Now, since the whales had surfaced to leeward, Derick and the other three German boats that soon followed him had a considerable head start on the Pequod's boats. There were eight whales, an average pod. Aware of their danger, they were swimming abreast at great speed straight before the wind, rubbing their flanks as closely as a team of horses in harness. They left a great, wide wake behind them, as though continually unrolling a vast parchment upon the sea.

Far behind in this rapid wake swam a huge, humped old bull. His comparatively slow progress and the unusual yellowish growths covering him made him seem afflicted with jaundice or some other infirmity. Whether this whale belonged to the pod ahead was questionable, for it is not customary for such ancient leviathans to be social. Nevertheless, he stuck to their wake, though their backwater must have slowed him, because the white foam at his broad muzzle was broken and choppy, like the swell formed when two opposing currents meet. His spout was short, slow, and labored — coming forth with a choking sort of gush and spending itself in torn shreds, followed by strange subterranean rumblings inside him that seemed to find their exit at his other buried end, causing the waters behind him to bubble up.

"Who's got some medicine?" said Stubb. "He has the stomach-ache, I'm afraid. Lord, think of having half an acre of stomach-ache! Wild winds are having a mad party inside him, boys. It's the first foul wind I ever knew to blow from astern. But look — did a whale ever steer so badly before? He must have lost his rudder."

As an overloaded merchant ship bearing down the coast of India with a deck full of frightened horses careens, buries, rolls, and wallows on her way — so did this old whale heave his aged bulk. Now and then, partly turning over on his cumbersome ribs, he exposed the cause of his unsteady wake: the unnatural stump of his starboard fin. Whether he had lost that fin in battle or had been born without it was hard to say.
"Only wait a bit, old chap, and I'll give you a sling for that wounded arm," cried cruel Flask, pointing to the whale-line near him.
"Watch he doesn't sling you with it," cried Starbuck. "Give way, or the German will have him."

With single purpose, all the rival boats were pointed toward this one whale. Not only was he the largest and therefore the most valuable, but he was nearest to them. The other whales were swimming with such great speed as to almost defy pursuit for the time being. At this point, the Pequod's boats had shot past the three German boats that launched last. But from the great head start he had, Derick's boat still led the chase, though his foreign rivals closed in with every moment. The only thing they feared was that, being already so close to the whale, he would manage to dart his iron before they could completely overtake and pass him. As for Derick, he seemed quite confident this would be the case, and occasionally shook his lamp-feeder at the other boats with a mocking gesture.

"The ungracious and ungrateful dog!" cried Starbuck. "He mocks and taunts me with the very charity box I filled for him not five minutes ago!" Then in his old intense whisper: "Give way, greyhounds! Go for it!"

"I tell you what it is, men," cried Stubb to his crew. "It's against my religion to get mad. But I'd like to eat that villainous German. Pull — won't you? Are you going to let that rascal beat you? Do you love brandy? A whole barrel of brandy to the best man. Come, why don't some of you burst a blood-vessel? Who's been dropping an anchor overboard? We don't budge an inch — we're dead in the water. Look, there's grass growing on the boat's bottom, and by the Lord, the mast is budding. This won't do, boys. Look at that German! The short and long of it is, men — will you spit fire or not?"

"Oh, see the foam he makes!" cried Flask, dancing up and down. "What a hump! Oh, do pile on the muscle — he lies like a log! Oh, my lads, do spring! Flapjacks and clams for supper, you know, my lads — baked clams and muffins! Oh, do, do spring! He's a hundred-barrel whale! Don't lose him now — don't, oh, don't! See that German! Oh, won't you pull for your pudding, my lads? Such a prize! Such a beauty! Don't you love spermaceti? There goes three thousand dollars, men! A bank! A whole bank! The Bank of England! Oh, do, do, do! What's that German about now?"

At this moment Derick was in the act of pitching his lamp-feeder at the advancing boats, and also his oil-can — perhaps with the double purpose of slowing his rivals' progress while accelerating his own through the backward momentum of the throw.

"The unmannerly Dutch mongrel!" cried Stubb. "Pull now, men, like fifty thousand shiploads of red-haired devils. What do you say, Tashtego — are you the man to snap your spine in twenty-two pieces for the honor of old Gay Head? What do you say?"
"I say, pull like god-damn," cried the Indian.

Fiercely but evenly spurred on by the Germans' taunts, the Pequod's three boats now began ranging almost abreast, and in that formation they steadily closed the gap. In that fine, loose, gallant stance of the headsman drawing near to his prey, the three mates stood up proudly, occasionally urging on the rear oarsman with an exhilarating cry: "There she slides now! Hurrah for the white-ash breeze! Down with the German! Sail over him!"

But Derick had such a decisive head start that despite all their courage, he would have won this race — had not righteous judgment descended upon him in the form of a crab that caught the blade of his middle oarsman. While this clumsy fellow was struggling to free his oar, and while Derick's boat was nearly capsizing as he thundered at his men in a mighty rage — that was the moment for Starbuck, Stubb, and Flask. With a shout, they surged forward and ranged up diagonally on the German's quarter. An instant more, and all four boats were in the whale's immediate wake, while stretching from them on both sides was the foaming swell the whale created.

It was a terrific, most pitiable, and maddening sight. The whale was now going head out, sending his spout before him in a continual tormented jet, while his one poor fin beat his side in an agony of fright. Now to this side, now to that, he swerved in his faltering flight. At every wave he broke, he either spasmodically sank into the sea or sideways rolled toward the sky his one beating fin. I have seen a bird with a clipped wing making frightened broken circles in the air, vainly trying to escape piratical hawks. But the bird has a voice, and with plaintive cries makes known her fear. But the fear of this vast dumb creature of the sea was chained up and enchanted in him. He had no voice save that choking respiration through his blowhole, and this made the sight of him unspeakably pitiable — while still, in his amazing bulk, his portcullis jaw, and his omnipotent tail, there was enough to terrify the bravest man who pitied him.

Seeing now that only a few more moments would give the Pequod's boats the advantage, and rather than be cheated of his prey, Derick chose to risk what must have seemed to him an unusually long throw before his last chance escaped forever.

But no sooner did his harpooner stand up for the strike than all three tigers — Queequeg, Tashtego, Daggoo — instinctively sprang to their feet. Standing in a diagonal row, they simultaneously aimed their barbs and darted over the head of the German harpooner. Their three Nantucket irons entered the whale. Blinding vapors of foam and white fire! The three boats, in the first fury of the whale's headlong rush, bumped the German's aside with such force that both Derick and his baffled harpooner were spilled out and sailed over by the three flying keels.

"Don't be afraid, my butter-boxes," cried Stubb, casting a passing glance at them as he shot by. "You'll be picked up presently — all right. I saw some sharks astern — St. Bernard's dogs, you know — they relieve distressed travelers. Hurrah! This is the way to sail now. Every keel a sunbeam! Hurrah! Here we go like three tin kettles at the tail of a mad cougar! This puts me in mind of being fastened to an elephant in a carriage on a plain — makes the wheel-spokes fly, boys, when you fasten to him that way. And there's danger of being pitched out, too, when you hit a hill. Hurrah! This is the way a fellow feels when he's going to Davy Jones — all a rush down an endless slope! Hurrah! This whale carries the everlasting mail!"

But the monster's run was brief. Giving a sudden gasp, he plunged straight down. With a grating rush, the three lines flew around the loggerheads with such force as to gouge deep grooves into them. The harpooners were so afraid this rapid sounding would soon exhaust the lines that they used all their skill to catch repeated smoking turns with the rope to hold on. At last — owing to the perpendicular strain from the lined chocks of the bows, where the three ropes went straight down into the blue — the gunwales of the bows were almost level with the water, while the three sterns tilted high in the air. When the whale stopped sounding, they remained in that position for a time, afraid to let out more line, though the situation was precarious. Boats have been pulled down and lost this way, yet it is this "holding on" — this hooking up by the sharp barbs embedded in the whale's living flesh — that often torments the Leviathan into rising again to meet the sharp lance of his enemies. Yet the peril aside, it is doubtful whether this is always the best course. It is reasonable to assume that the longer the wounded whale stays underwater, the more he is exhausted. Because of the enormous surface area of a full-grown sperm whale — something less than two thousand square feet — the pressure of the water is immense. We all know what an astonishing atmospheric weight we ourselves bear, even here above ground in the air. How vast, then, the burden of a whale, bearing on his back a column of two hundred fathoms of ocean! It must at least equal the weight of fifty atmospheres. One whaleman has estimated it at the weight of twenty warships, with all their guns, stores, and men on board.

As the three boats lay there on that gently rolling sea, gazing down into its eternal blue noon — and as not a single groan or cry, not so much as a ripple or a bubble, came up from its depths — what landsman would have thought that beneath all that silence and peace, the greatest monster of the seas was writhing and wrenching in agony! Not eight inches of rope were visible at the bows. Can it be believed that by three such thin threads the great Leviathan was suspended like the weight of an eight-day clock? Suspended? And from what? From three bits of board. Is this the creature of whom it was once so triumphantly said: "Can you fill his skin with barbed irons? Or his head with fish-spears? The sword of him that strikes at him cannot hold; the spear, the dart, nor the coat of mail. He regards iron as straw; the arrow cannot make him flee; darts are counted as stubble; he laughs at the shaking of a spear!" This the creature? This he? Oh, that prophecies should go unfulfilled! For with the strength of a thousand thighs in his tail, Leviathan had run his head under the mountains of the sea to hide from the Pequod's spears!

In that sloping afternoon sunlight, the shadows that the three boats cast beneath the surface must have been long enough and broad enough to shade half of Xerxes' army. Who can tell how terrifying those huge phantoms must have been, flitting over the wounded whale's head!

"Stand by, men — he stirs," cried Starbuck, as the three lines suddenly vibrated in the water, conducting upward to them like magnetic wires the life-and-death throbs of the whale. Every oarsman felt them in his seat. The next moment, largely relieved from the downward strain at the bows, the boats gave a sudden bounce upward, like a small ice field when a dense herd of polar bears is scared off it into the sea.
"Haul in! Haul in!" cried Starbuck again. "He's rising."

The lines, of which hardly an instant before not a hand's breadth could have been gained, were now flung back in long, quick coils, dripping, into the boats. Soon the whale broke the surface within two ship-lengths of the hunters.

His movements clearly showed his extreme exhaustion. In most land animals, there are certain valves in their veins that, when the animal is wounded, at least partly shut off the blood flow in certain directions. Not so with the whale. One of his peculiarities is a completely non-valvular blood-vessel structure, so that when pierced by even so small a point as a harpoon, a deadly drain begins at once upon his whole arterial system. When this is worsened by the extraordinary water pressure at great depth below the surface, his life may be said to pour from him in constant streams. Yet so vast is the quantity of blood in him, and so distant and numerous its interior sources, that he will keep bleeding for a considerable period — even as a river will flow during a drought whose source lies in the hidden springs of far-off hills. Even now, when the boats closed on this whale and dangerously drew over his swaying flukes, and the lances were thrust into him, they were followed by steady jets from the new wounds, which kept continually playing, while the natural spout-hole in his head only sent its frightened moisture into the air at intervals, however rapid. From this last vent no blood yet came, because no vital part had been struck. His life, as they significantly call it, was untouched.

As the boats now more closely surrounded him, the whole upper part of his body, including much that is normally submerged, was plainly revealed. His eyes — or rather the places where his eyes had been — were visible. As strange, misshapen growths gather in the knotholes of the noblest oaks when they lie fallen, so from the spots where the whale's eyes had once been, there now protruded blind bulbs, horribly pitiable to see. But pity there was none. For all his old age, his one fin, and his blind eyes, he must die and be murdered — in order to light the gay weddings and other celebrations of men, and also to illuminate the solemn churches that preach unconditional gentleness to all. Still rolling in his blood, at last he partly revealed a strangely discolored lump or swelling, the size of a bushel, low on his flank.
"A nice spot," cried Flask. "Just let me prick him there once."
"Hold off!" cried Starbuck. "There's no need of that!"

But humane Starbuck was too late. The instant the dart struck, an ulcerous jet shot from that cruel wound. Goaded by it into more than bearable agony, the whale — now spouting thick blood — blindly charged the boats with savage fury, spattering them and their gloating crews all over with showers of gore, capsizing Flask's boat and smashing the bows. It was his death stroke. For by this time, so drained was he from blood loss that he helplessly rolled away from the wreck he had made, lay panting on his side, and impotently flapped his stumped fin. Then over and over he slowly revolved like a dying world, turned up the white secrets of his belly, lay like a log, and died. It was most pitiable, that last expiring spout. As when unseen hands gradually draw the water from some mighty fountain, and with half-stifled, melancholy gurglings the spray-column lowers and lowers to the ground — so fell the last long dying spout of the whale.

Soon, while the crews waited for the ship to arrive, the body showed signs of sinking with all its treasures untouched. Immediately, by Starbuck's orders, lines were secured to it at different points, so that before long every boat served as a buoy, with the sunken whale suspended a few inches beneath them by the ropes. By very careful management, when the ship drew near, the whale was transferred to her side and strongly secured there by the stiffest fluke-chains. For it was clear that unless artificially held up, the body would sink at once to the bottom.

It happened that almost upon the first cut into him with the spade, the entire length of a corroded harpoon was found embedded in his flesh, on the lower part of the lump described before. But since the stumps of harpoons are frequently found in the dead bodies of captured whales, with the flesh perfectly healed around them and no sign of their location, there must have been some other unknown reason to explain the ulceration. But still more curious was the fact that a stone lance-head was found in him, not far from the buried iron, with the flesh perfectly firm around it. Who had thrown that stone lance? And when? It might have been hurled by some Northwest Indian long before America was discovered.

What other marvels might have been dug out of this monstrous cabinet there is no telling. But a sudden stop was put to further discoveries when the ship was unprecedentedly dragged sideways toward the sea, owing to the body's rapidly increasing tendency to sink. However, Starbuck, who was in charge, hung on to it to the last — hung on so stubbornly, in fact, that when at length the ship would have capsized if she kept holding on, and the command was given to break clear, the strain upon the timber-heads to which the fluke-chains and cables were fastened was so immense that it was impossible to cast them off. Meanwhile, everything in the Pequod was tilted at an angle. To cross to the other side of the deck was like walking up the steep gabled roof of a house. The ship groaned and gasped. Many of the ivory inlays in her bulwarks and cabins were popped from their places by the unnatural dislocation. In vain, handspikes and crowbars were brought to bear upon the immovable fluke-chains to pry them loose from the timber-heads. The submerged ends could not be reached at all, while every moment whole tons of weight seemed to be added to the sinking mass, and the ship seemed on the point of going over.

"Hold on, hold on, won't you?" cried Stubb to the body. "Don't be in such a devil of a hurry to sink! By thunder, men, we must do something or we're done for. No use prying there. Stop it, I say, with your handspikes, and one of you run for a prayer book and a pen-knife and cut the big chains."

"Knife? Aye, aye," cried Queequeg, and seizing the carpenter's heavy hatchet, he leaned out of a porthole and, steel against iron, began slashing at the largest fluke-chains. But only a few strokes, full of sparks, were needed before the tremendous strain did the rest. With a terrific snap, every fastening broke loose. The ship righted. The carcass sank.

Now, this occasional inevitable sinking of the recently killed sperm whale is a very curious thing. No fisherman has yet adequately explained it. Usually the dead sperm whale floats with great buoyancy, its side or belly considerably elevated above the surface. If the only whales that sank this way were old, meager, broken-hearted creatures, with their pads of fat diminished and all their bones heavy and rheumatic, then you might reasonably argue that this sinking is caused by an uncommon density in the whale. But it is not so. For young whales in the peak of health, swelling with noble energy, prematurely cut off in the warm flush and springtime of life with all their plump fat about them — even these strong, buoyant heroes sometimes sink.

It should be said, however, that the sperm whale is far less prone to this than any other species. Where one sperm whale goes down, twenty right whales do. This difference is no doubt largely due to the greater quantity of bone in the right whale. Its baleen plates alone sometimes weigh more than a ton, and from this burden the sperm whale is wholly free. But there are instances where, after many hours or several days, the sunken whale rises again, more buoyant than in life. The reason is obvious. Gases are generated inside him. He swells to prodigious size and becomes a sort of animal balloon. A warship could hardly keep him under then. In the shore whaling, in the shallows among the bays of New Zealand, when a right whale shows signs of sinking, they fasten buoys to him with plenty of rope, so that when the body has gone down, they know where to look for it when it rises again.

It was not long after the sinking of the body that a cry was heard from the Pequod's mastheads, announcing that the Jungfrau was again lowering her boats — though the only spout in sight was that of a fin-back, a species of whale that is virtually impossible to capture because of its incredible swimming speed. Nevertheless, the fin-back's spout is so similar to the sperm whale's that unskilled fishermen often mistake it. And so Derick and all his men were now in valiant chase of this uncatchable brute. The Virgin, crowding on all sail, followed after her four boats, and they all disappeared far to leeward, still in bold, hopeful pursuit.
Oh! Many are the fin-backs, and many are the Dericks, my friend.
